newsitem.title: GERMANY: GErman metal union boss attacks Bonn government.
newsitem.headline: GErman metal union boss attacks Bonn government.

text.p: Klaus Zwickel, leader of Germany's IG Metall metal and engineering union, on Friday launched a fierce attack against Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government and its austerity deficit-cutting measures.

Zwickel, speaking at a workers' welfare conference, described the cuts in the programme as socially unfair and concentrating budget cuts on the less-privileged while easing the tax burden on the rich.
"This country can no longer afford such backward-looking policies. This country needs a new parliamentary majority," Zwickel said in his most outspoken attack on the government yet.

Kohl and Finance Minister Theo Waigel have pushed through parliament the austerity package aimed at whipping Germany's finances into shape to meet entry criteria for the single European currency, which is slated to start in 1999.

In reference to a recent comment by Kohl that the previous target of halving unemployment to around two million people by the year 2000 was optimistic, Zwickel insisted that such a reduction should still be the goal.
He said cuts in overtime worked would alone create around one million jobs within two years, while a general 35-hour working week would add a further 400,000 jobs.

Zwickel, whose union has led protests involving hundreds of thousands of metal workers against sick pay cuts envisaged by the austerity package, said IG Metall would keep up its fight against the cuts to worker benefits.

In an interview before his speech, Zwickel downplayed attempts by union negotiators in the southwestern state of Baden-Wuerttemberg to find a "pilot" agreement that could be used as a model for 1997 wage agreements.
"There is no obligation on them to find such a pilot deal," Zwickel told Reuters.
He added that any agreement reached in the state, home to German industrial group Daimler-Benz AG, would have to be evaluated on its merit.

Central talks between IG Metall and the Gesamtmetall engineering employers federation broke down earlier this month with one of the main sticking points being the proposed 20 percent cut in sick pay benefits.
